p:
On the other hand, we really want to be clear that for large corporate entities that really have no excuse to not understand what the law is, we're going to take a really tough line. We're going to insist that when large corporate actors rip off New Yorkers, that they not only pay them back, but that they pay a civil penalty to the

City of New York. So, it's really about making sure that small businesses aren't being beaten up through taxes and fines and fees, but also making sure there's real accountability when large corporate actors make a conscious decision to break the law.

I would just add, I think this was referenced by my colleague, Mike Tiger, earlier, but we have always taken a very proactive stance on how we can reduce fines and fees, even outside of executive orders. And I can think of most recently toward the end of last session working with Chairman at the time, now Speaker Menin, to reform many of our license categories, removing anachronistic license categories, removing certain requirements to get a license that ultimately save folks hundreds of thousands of dollars in fees.
Okay. And then just finally, the issue of licensed versus unlicensed industries. Do you break down the complaints that way, or that's not something that you do?

This is a good question, Council Member. It's not exactly how we break it down, but we do have industry by industry. You know, we do have a rough outline of industries

that are unlicensed where we get a number of complaints. So for example, car wash is a big category we get hundreds of complaints about, tobacco retail dealer, another big category, electronic cigarette dealer. And we, you know, are always open to conversations with the Council about whether licensing might be appropriate given the volume of complaints we're receiving.

Yeah. And just to be clear, there are two ways you can look at it, and I just want for clarity. There is licensed, so say tobacco retail dealers. There are charges that we have under licensing law. You're a licensed tobacco retail dealer, and we charge it. And then there are tobacco retail dealers that are unlicensed. And then there are non-licensed entities, entities that don't require a license. So those are, like, the three different buckets within. And as I said in response to an earlier question, we're always willing to engage with you and your staff to sort of carve up the numbers in a way that you think would be helpful to have a discussion.

Are there industries as you're doing this that should be

licensed that are not licensed, or you don't really have that kind of insight?

I think that's something we want to get back to you on, but I could give you an example of where that's been successful. We were receiving, I think, hundreds of complaints every year about self-storage. And then last year the Council made self-storage a license category. We now have a much better ability to stop abuses in that field. I thought the problem was so bad, that was what prompted us to bring a major lawsuit a couple weeks ago against Extra Space. So, we're definitely proactively looking for categories of complaints where we're seeing major problems, and we'd be happy to work with you to talk about where a licensing regime might be appropriate.
One last question.
Gale, can we…

I just want to ask about newsstands quickly. They are no longer selling newspapers. So down the line, I'd love to hear your input as to what they should be doing because it's not really fair for them to get a summons when

there's no newspaper that anybody's going to read. So something to think about.
Yeah. And that's an ongoing conversation we're having as well.
Okay. Thank you.
We see it every day.
Thanks. I know Council Member Aldebol, Shirley, do you have questions still, and then I'll do Council Member Ossé after.

Yes. I did have a quick question about when you provide education to small businesses, do you coordinate with other agencies like Small Business Services, that, you know, provide or even our Business Improvement Districts, to provide information to the smaller businesses.

Oh, absolutely, Council Member. I'll say briefly, and I'll turn it over to my colleague. We absolutely coordinate with SBS and other agencies. I've already had meetings with Business Improvement Districts where we've started making plans to do business education pitches

in BIDs. We love having partners that help us get the word out. And Carlos, you should add to that.

Yeah. I think the most discrete example we have perhaps is our business education days outreach model where we go and canvas corridors of small businesses with SBS, with local BIDs to provide information one-on-one to businesses. And we welcome doing those events as well with the local Council Members. I think it's a great way for us to engage as a team to educate small businesses.
Thank you.

Thank you. And I want to acknowledge also Council Member De La Rosa is with us and Council Member Ossé, welcome, and yeah, please go ahead. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: (INAUDIBLE) we were going to be able to ask a question after all of Council Member Brewer's amazing questions, but I'm glad I got an opportunity. Good afternoon, Chair and Commissioner, as well Carlos as well as the rest of the DCWP team. I wanted to ask a question around rideshare within the City of New York. You know, in

the past, there have been rules adopted under the Consumer Protections Law that addressed price gouging and hidden fees. I also know that the Mamdani Administration is working to tackle the issue of junk fees as a whole. And many New Yorkers are concerned about price discrepancies and surcharges for rideshares like Uber and Lyft. The same ride from one destination to another can have a different price, and there is no real transparency from such companies on how these costs are calculated. In Chicago, it was found that rideshare apps and delivery service apps were overcharging users and we may be seeing the same thing in New York City. What is DCWP’s plan to tackle surcharges and rideshare pricing, and how can the agency ensure we end the use of surcharging as a whole?

Yeah. I think this is an outstanding question, Council Member. And I think one of the reasons it’s so important to get this right is because what we are seeing in the rideshare industry, what we’ve been seeing for years, which is to say personalized pricing that’s always changing in unpredictable ways. The three of us could all request certain rideshare right now to the same

spot and get three entirely different prices, and for too long these companies have made these pricing decisions in a block box without any transparency by the public or by the public. But why this is so important is because while the rideshare industry has pioneered this work, it is spreading. We’ve already great reporting of how Instacart, for example, appears to be engaging in all forms of price discrimination and price experimentation. We know that the airlines have long been engaged in price experimentation. And there’s a big concern out there that grocery stores, especially as they start to incorporate electronic shelf labels, could start using biometric surveillance and electronic shelf labels to engage in their own kind of surgery pricing and dynamic pricing. We are certainly looking every day at where our existing authorities can tackle the biggest harms. For example, if prices aren’t being clearly posted, if consumers are being deceived, if they’re being offered discounts that aren’t real, this is something we take very seriously. But we’d also be very pleased to work with you and work with the Council on more comprehensive legislation to reign in these practices.

And I would identify at least two practices that probably merit the Council’s attention because they are distinct. One is dynamic pricing, when companies are constantly changing prices throughout the day. That’s often what leads to the kind of price gouging I think you and most of us have experienced out in the real world. We know that Speaker Menin has spoken about this issue as well. And the other is what the FTC, my former agency, has called surveillance pricing, and that’s making pricing decisions based on an individual’s personal data, which raises both economic fairness and privacy concerns. I believe that addressing emerging forms of pricing abuses requires addressing both of these, dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing, and it’s something we’re giving a lot of thought to, both under our existing authority and we’re giving thought to how the Council might tackle this directly. So, that should be an ongoing conversation I hope. We do have some ideas on it, and we look forward to working with you on it. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: I appreciate that. And I definitely have some ideas around it too and

would love to get together offline to discuss how we can hold some of these companies accountable.
Yes. Thank you.

Thank you, Council Member Ossé. I assume that’s it? Okay. I dont see any more hands. If I can, I’ll dig in for a couple more questions for you. When I say a couple, a few, if that’s okay, Commissioner?
Of course.

I’d like to talk to you about language capacity because, you know, obviously New York is a multicultural city. Can you break down the complaints, how many of them are from English as first language speakers or non-English first language speakers?

I am seeing if I have those figures, Council Member, and while my colleagues help me to see if we do, I can tell you that we do accept complaints in complaints in about a dozen languages, and for those languages we can’t support, we have additional tools that we deploy to accept those complaints as well.

It looks like we don’t have those at the ready. I apologize, Mr. Chairman, but we’re happy to get you those.

Yeah. It would be great to know, like, who's complaining. Like, are we getting older adults complaining, people under 30, non-English speakers. It would be great to see who is getting access to you and who is not, so the things that we need to be doing to make your services available to a population that might otherwise be complaining but don’t know. I think that would be great for us to have that information.

I’m happy to do that, Council Member. If I could just follow up very briefly. When I was in Washington, we did do research into this, and what we found is that folks who don’t speak English, folks who don’t make as much money, and people of color often are less likely to file complaints. That is a big problem because what that means is that the agencies aren’t doing the necessary enforcement to protect some of our most vulnerable communities. So, one of my priorities as Commissioner, and Carlos has been an outstanding leader on this, is getting out. We’re not just

sitting here in our office… today, we’re just going to be sitting here in our office… but most days we’re not just sitting here in our office waiting for complaints to come in. We’re doing about two events a day is our goal this year all over New York City, every borough, to try to hear from people directly about what they’re seeing on the ground, including immigrant communities that might not feel comfortable filing complaints themselves but can work with partners to bring issues to our attention. So, we’re happy to get you whatever numbers we can, but I see it as fundamental to our work to not just wait for complaints to come in but to go out into communities and hear from people directly.
Yeah. And great to know how we use our resources to do that, like hiring non-profit partners who –
Yes.

– have relationships in communities, especially non-English-speaking communities who would have language capacity to help people understand the issues and demystify DCWP for them as well. Let’s see how much resources we’re

spending there and if we need to put additional resources into those communities.

Chair, if I could as well. I think language capacity, to the Commissioner’s point, has always been a major priority for our agency in terms of the communities that we need to reach. Within our outreach team alone, we have team members that combined, we speak seven or eight languages. The agency overall, if you look at all of our staffers, we have close to 40 languages that are spoken. Half of the agency has the ability to speak a language other than English as well. I think it’s something that we have long prioritized at this agency because we know that’s how we engage with folks out there. And in terms of our outreach model, again, our goal is to be able to say we’ve hit two outreach events per day throughout the year.
The weather’s not helped that.

But a big part of that model, for sure, is tapping into organizations, community-based organizations, going to their monthly meetings. Being accessible as much

as possible to make sure that we’re reaching every community we can.

That’d be great, and it’d be great to see what kind of outreach efforts and how we, as a Council, could be helpful with those outreach efforts. If there are things that we could be doing, I’m happy to reach out to, you know, people on our Committee and, you know, to help figure out how we can do more events together to get to, you know, hard to reach communities.

Thank you, Council Member. We would love to do that. And we already greatly appreciate the work that you’ve done to broadcast our free tax prep program now, particularly as we’re looking to cut down fees for New Yorkers and make sure that they have trusted available resources to them.

Yeah. Sure. And can I ask you, I know Council Member Brewer raised the issue of complaints that are of licensed versus unlicensed industries. Do you have a breakdown of how much of the 27,000 complaints are coming from people who are unlicensed or unlicensed vendors or unlicensed industries.

Just to clarify, because I think we’re going to have to follow up. Do you mean complaints about industries that should be licensed but are, in fact, unlicensed, or complaints from industries that are just outside our licensing categories?
Commissioner, I would say both would be helpful, honestly –
Okay.

– because if we see, you know, I think we all read that article in The City I think around the tow trucks, the unlicensed tow trucks, right, so it’s a licensed industry with a lot of unlicensed people versus an industry that might be an unlicensed industry where we’re seeing a lot of consumer complaints. I think both are really going to be helpful for us.

Yeah. So, I think the numbers I was referring to earlier were industries that should be licensed but we’re seeing a lot of unlicensed. I think we need to follow up on both of those, but we’re happy to do that.

Great. Thank you. I appreciate that.

And so can we talk about restitution. You mentioned that your goal is to get people restitution. Do you have numbers for ‘24 and ‘25 of how many of the 27,000 cases resulted in a restitution for the complainant.
Well, I know in the past four years, we’ve secured more than 28 million dollars in restitution disbursements and debt relief. I don’t know, let me see if we have the numbers for the last two years.

Yeah. Or even what percentage of the complaints got restitution. I mean it would be great if everyone got restitution. I’m sure it’s kind of weighted on some of the bigger cases got larger restitution, and maybe some people got no restitution.

I don’t know if we track it by the number of complaints. I can tell you in 2024 we secured 4.2 million in restitution, 2023, 1 million in restitution. One thing to keep in mind, though, is that, you know, we do a lot of mediation of complaints where we don’t always track that number in restitution as we would in enforcement.

I know our consumer services mediators, I think last year got between 300,000 and 400,000 dollars in restitution, and that’s incorporated into the total that the Commissioner mentioned before, 4.2 million overall, by the agency, whether it be through mediation or the efforts of our attorneys through investigations.

Yeah. I mean, that’s wonderful. It’d be great to know, if you can, what percentages of the overall total resulted in restitution or some kind of mediation with some restitution for the individual. It’s great for us to kind of have that for that data as well. If of the 27,000, 20,000 people, through mediation or litigation, got restitution, it’s very different than if 2,000 people did.
We’ll get those numbers for you, Chair. And just so I can clarify, last year, 2025, 3.1 million in restitution, and 430,00 of that was through mediation.

That’s great numbers. That’s really a lot of money back to New Yorkers so I do appreciate that.

And in ‘24 and ‘25, (INAUDIBLE) filed a lot of requests to OATH. Do you have how many of those applications went to OATH versus what you’ve resolved through mediation.
I believe, how many applications went to OATH. I believe, let’s see, we had 17,000 summons. Do you know the answer to that, Mike?
How many summonses went to OATH? We had 17,000 summonses overall. All our cases, except for the handful bigger investigations that go to State court, they all are returnable to
So, 17,000 out of the overall 27,000 went to OATH for some kind of deliberation?

No. There’s 27,000 complaints the agency received last year. Last year, we issued 17,000 summonses, and all of those summonses are returnable to OATH, barring a handful that my colleague mentioned that could go to other venues as well.

But just to be clear, there are Venn diagrams that are operating. They are not one-to-one necessarily. Not every complaint is something that would generate an inspection, that would generate a summons. Depends on what the consumer actually wants.
I think that’s right. The substance of the complaint will lead to a different pathway, depending on the needs of the consumer.

And there are summonses we issue that are not from consumer complaints. So, again, that’s why I say we can sort of work with your Staff to dissect however way you think it would be helpful for your and your team to sort of engage, but I just want to set those parameters that there’s not just one pipeline.

Yeah. At least for me, I mean, it’s great to know how many of these are resolved through mediation then if you’re handing it off to OATH, how OATH is resolving these, and if there’s any bottleneck for the consumer who is trying to get some resolve. It’s really good to hear that you’re hearing something, came back within a short

period of time, and resolving most of it in 90 days. But let’s say it’s getting stuck at OATH, that’s also important for us to hear as well.

And I can say, Chair, that is certainly a priority for me as well. I want to be sure that when we’re committing resources to enforcement that we can move relatively quickly. I don’t want, you know, one thing you’ve seen this year, for example, is a willingness to file cases in State court, like the action we just filed against Extra Space. All options are on the table when it comes to making sure we’re resolving these cases as quickly as possible, getting money back in the consumers’ pockets. I don’t like to see cases drag on for years.

And, Chair, just to confirm as well. Last year, we conducted 2,100 mediations. In addition, of complaints we received last year, 3,000 were referred for inspection that the Commissioner mentioned earlier. So, that’s kind of a little bit of the breakdown right now that we have.

That’s good information.

We’ve seen a lot in grocery retail, a lot of complaints under the CPL. Do you have any sense of why there’s been such an increase in this category of charges filed under the CPL for grocery retail establishments?

My sense is that people are getting really frustrated with what they’re dealing with at the grocery store. I mean, obviously they’re frustrated with the higher prices, but what our inspectors are finding is a lot of pretty serious violations at times. So, for example, we’ve seen a lot of inspectors come back and tell us that grocery stores are charging tax on non-taxable items, like feminine hygiene products or over-the-counter medicines. We’ve seen failure to disclose credit card fees and credit card limitations. We’re seeing sale of expired medication. So, you know, we get complaints for all sorts of reasons, but our inspectors on their own are finding that some of the core protections grocery shoppers are entitled to are not being honored.

I’d also mention, Chair, that, you know, as we were referencing earlier with Council Member Brewer’s

questions, over the past few years we have had to prioritize inspections of places that are selling tobacco products. Oftentimes, these might overlap. You know, a bodega, for example, with a grocery store selling tobacco. It brings us to that place in the first place and where we’re also looking at other violations that might be popping up during the course of those inspections. So, I think it’s part and parcel informed by what’s happening in the marketplace, complaints we’re receiving guiding our enforcement efforts to certain places.

Just one other point. Sorry. Boring data nerd. Flag here is that over time, depending on sort of changes made to our internal tracking databases, and other things, we may be charging the statute, which is the CPL 20-700 of the Administrative Code, but we’ve promulgated a ton of rules including some of our core meat and potatoes consumer protections, and sometimes, in some years we charge the statute, sometimes we charge the rules, and so that’s, again, I just want to offer sort of our services and work with your Staff to sort of dice the numbers the way we think is best. Because I think just a caution, we don’t want to sort of overanalyze

just looking at these data in the first instance and want to look underneath them to make sure they’re actually reflecting what we’re, you know, what our intuition is.

Yeah. We’d love to do that. I appreciate that offer. I look forward to doing that with our teams. Can I turn our attention to kind of online deceptive practices? Obviously, this has been a growing portion of your work. Can you tell us, you know, how you've been addressing this issue? Do you see, you know, increasing complaints, whether it's cryptocurrency, online deceptive practices? Can you tell us what you're seeing now?

Yeah. I mean, so much fraud today is moving online, and so many of the problems we see are driven by digital interface. So, I'll just give you one example, Council Member, of how we're trying to get ahead of that. One of the initiatives the Mayor launched in, I believe, second week, I think, was this executive order on subscription traps. And, you know, subscription traps is a name, it means different things to different people, but where I've seen it is companies that

market themselves online, and they say, just click here and you'll sign up for a subscription. There'll be a three week, you know, free trial, and then there's $1.99 a month, and there's a little asterisk. And then if you actually read the fine print, it says we're going to start charging 40 dollars a month on month two, month three, month four. One of the things the Mayor said is directing DCWP to put an end to that. You saw last week, he sent warnings to gyms across the city. But we know that many of the deceptive practices we see are not actually in the gym, they're online. The Federal Trade Commission just sued LA Fitness for using online deception to trap people in subscriptions. You know, we see a similar dynamic in our junk fee work. Digital pricing has enabled a vast number of companies to engage in what used to be called drip pricing, where companies advertise one price, say on booking.com or Priceline, and then you click through, you enter your credit card information, you go through the whole process, and 10 minutes later, you realize, oh, there's a 40-dollar resort fee on the back end. So, we finalized, and you were there for this announcement along with Council Member Brewer and the Mayor, on

the strongest in the nation hotel junk fee rule to require upfront advertising of prices. So, we really are, and I have a track record of this going back to my work in D.C., working to make sure that our consumer protection laws keep pace with technology. At the end of the day, what's deceptive in person is also deceptive online. I think what's really changed is that companies have new techniques, new tricks that they can use online to get people, and that's why we're really trying to modernize our enforcement and make sure that both our rules and our enforcement reflect the reality of what consumers are experiencing in the marketplace.

Just a couple other specific instances that we've been working on over the last couple of years and that the Commissioner is really sort of taking the leadership mantle to push us to do even more. We had a case that we filed in state Supreme Court that's still pending against Dorm2Dorm, a moving company that was targeting students online for moving services, but not giving them the benefit of their bargain. That's a case that's still pending in state court. We have a case against way.com. One thing that is really

interesting here is how online actors can supercharge the deception of brick and mortar and smaller online actors and say, oh, maybe I'd be skeptical if I was just seeing this on the street, but with this patina of credibility of this major website, then, oh, I will actually go through and then consumers are very prompt and we're very attuned to making sure that websites are not supercharging and thinking creatively how we can get around the federal laws that the Commissioner was alluding to about 20 minutes ago with great vigor about the problem that's happening with federal policy about online actors. But we went after way.com because they were actually acting as a booking agent for unlicensed garages, and that's a real problem we've seen, especially in Southeast Queens around JFK. And we've also had a lot of enforcement around lithium-ion batteries. That was something that we've worked with the Council a great deal over the last couple of years, and that wasn't just about brick and mortar locations, but also online actors. So, we always have an eye to not just what's going on on the streets, but what's also going on the internet as far as deceiving New Yorkers.

Thank you. Thank you. I also want to acknowledge that Council Member Krishnan is here too. I want to thank him for joining us. I'm going to do two more questions and I'll do other Council Members two questions. So, we've heard a lot about small businesses, and do you see a lot of small businesses who are victims of abusive and deceptive practice, and what do you think your role is in protecting those small businesses from kind of larger business who are engaging in that deception?

Yeah. Absolutely, Chair. You know, the reality is that small businesses are getting scammed just like ordinary people are getting scammed. After all, small businesses are led by people. We have scammers going door to door, marketing payment systems to small businesses that are often frauds. Small businesses get trapped in subscriptions just like the rest of us do. Small businesses have to deal with junk fees just like the rest of us do. One thing I've heard a lot from small businesses I've spoken with is that, you know, a

small business might be next to a Target or another big box store and that small business pays more, say, for Pepsi than the Target right next to them, and how is that small business supposed to compete when these big distributors are discriminating against them, charging more than neighboring stores? So, I think it's a huge problem. Unfortunately, our Consumer Protection Law is limited to follow the CFPB standard at the federal level, which is personal or household use. That sometimes limits the types of cases we can bring. But I absolutely believe there's a need for greater accountability when small businesses are targeted. We'd be delighted to work with you, to work with the Council, to make sure that small businesses actually have tools to fight back when they're being scammed and to fight back against the kind of price discrimination and other abuses that are driving far too many businesses out of the city.

One case, you know, the Commissioner alluded to sort of the limitations of our current Consumer Protection Law and that phrase, personal household or family goods. I can give you one example of how we have helped small businesses. Recently, a couple of years ago,

the Council passed a suite of regulations and a licensing scheme for third-party food delivery services. And we filed a case last year at OATH against Hungry Panda, and the people who are being protected there are small restaurants because they were being charged above what the fee cap that this Council passed permits, and that's a case that we have pursued at OATH. So that's a case where we did have a law and we were very vigorous in pursuing that to protect small businesses.
Thank you. Council Member Aldebol.

Yeah. In addition to fines, what other ways can you deal with violations, you know, consumer scams or price gouging? Is there a requirement for someone who violates the consumer's rights to post something in their establishment or on their website, kind of laying out what consumer's rights are?

Yeah. This is an excellent question, and it's something I think about a lot. Let's say we catch a company breaking the law, ripping off consumers. How do we make sure it doesn't happen again? You know, for a lot of these big

companies out there, they can pay 10,000 dollars. Some companies can pay a billion dollars and not think twice about it and go around, break the law again the next day because it's not a big deal to them. So, I think about a number of tools that we have I think that we are already using to make sure that companies are actually deterred from ripping off New Yorkers. One thing that has been a big theme throughout my enforcement career and that I'm very much prioritizing here at DCWP is individual accountability. You know, in my last job, we sued Amazon for ripping people off and trapping people in subscription, but Amazon can write a big check and not care. That's why we named three Amazon executives personally to make sure that they got the message that ripping off the American people was off limits and wouldn't be tolerated. I think that sends a strong message to the industry. That's something we're already doing here at DCWP, whether it's our case against Radiant Solar, our case against Motoclick. We are naming individuals when appropriate, not only to make sure that the message that's sent, that individuals can be liable for cheating people, for cheating workers, but also

because to the point we were talking about earlier, we want to make sure we can actually get money back to consumers at the end of the day. That means that if a CEO or an executive runs off with millions of dollars of consumers' money, we want to be able to get the judgment against that individual and get that money back into consumers' pockets. You also raised, Council Member, you know, what kind of other relief can we require? Notices, injunctive relief. Another thing that we are doing more and more at DCWP is filing cases in State court instead of filing them at OATH. What that allows us to do is ask the judge to actually issue injunctions, order businesses sometimes permanently to stop breaking the law, order businesses sometime, I have seen this, to notify customers about what happened and send them checks for refunds. That's exactly the kind of relief we have found. You know, when businesses actually have to tell their customers, you got ripped off and now we got sued, we're making you whole, that can send a really important message to the public that New York City has their back and to other businesses that they shouldn't rip off the people of this city. So, we would welcome the opportunity to work with your

office to think about the kind of remedies, the kind of interventions that actually stop fraud and that deter fraud, and that is one reason we're bringing more cases in State court, naming more individuals. We want the message to get out of the era of ripping people off is over.

Shirley, anything else? Okay. Great. Can I turn my attention to Intro. 177? Can you tell us, and I appreciate your support of that Introduction, if this bill gets signed into law, how would your agency use this? How could you integrate it into City's financial empowerment centers? Kind of how could this be an additional tool for consumers around student loans?

Yeah. So, we're excited about this law. And as you referenced, there's a lot we're already doing for student loan borrowers. We do our financial empowerment centers where we provide one-on-one counseling to thousands of New Yorkers every year, including on their student loans. We have a pilot program with Summer where we're offering both for New York City employees and

New Yorkers the opportunity to enroll in public service loan forgiveness or income-driven repayment. We do enforcement against predatory colleges, like we brought a case against Berkeley College, recovering more than 20 million dollars in debt relief for students. We do outreach and education, including when we thought that there was going to be student loan garnishment at the beginning part of this year. We're going to launch a major outreach effort. But I think to your point, we need to align those efforts to make sure we're serving as many New Yorkers as we can. We know that between 1 and 1.4 New Yorkers are burdened by student loans. We know that far too many of those New Yorkers are likely facing default. So, we really need a coordinated, all-hands-on-deck effort, not only within DCWP, but coordinating with outside partners to serve as many New Yorkers as we can who are struggling with student loans. And I think Intro. 177 would be the vehicle to do just that, to make sure we're coordinating our efforts, we're being strategic about reaching us. There's a lot more people we need to reach, and I think this is going to help turbocharge our efforts.

Thank you, Commissioner. And I appreciate on 410, really wanting to figure out how we can make this work. I appreciate Council Member Riley's bill here. Have you seen complaints around this issue on flexible benefits cards at retail establishments? Have you heard from consumers at all?

No. I don't think we've received formal complaints, but that might be because people don't know to complain. I will say, Chair, that I recognize this is a very real problem that the Council Member is looking to address. We know that people have these flex benefits, and at the end of the year, they often lose their flex benefits because they expire and people don't know where to use them. So, I completely agree with the notion that to make the city more affordable, let's make sure New Yorkers can take advantage of the benefits they already have, rather than just letting these benefits line the profits of big insurance companies that have made billions of dollars off ripping off the people of New York City. I think the thing we want to make sure of, and we'd very much like to work with the Council on this, is this can be, we want to make sure

this doesn't impose a big cost on the small businesses of the city. I have heard so many complaints from small businesses, corner bodegas, about sky-high processing fees, credit card fees, they're already needing to pay.
